pages.x: In 1494 the French king Charles VIII marched the length of Italy to seize Naples. Ferdinand of Aragon sent his best soldier, Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, the Great Captain. In 1503 at Cerignola his arquebusiers, firing from behind a ditch, cut down the French knights, and Naples became Spanish for two hundred years.

Ferdinand's grandson Charles inherited Spain and its Italian kingdoms from his mother's family, and the Netherlands and Austria from his father's. In 1519 the German princes, well bribed, elected him Holy Roman Emperor. No ruler since Charlemagne had held so much of Europe, and France found itself surrounded.
From the 1530s Spain's foot soldiers were formed into tercios: permanent regiments of pikemen and men with guns, who trained and lived together and were paid, when the money came, from Spain.
pages.fx: For a century they were the most feared infantry in Europe, fighting from Tunis to the Netherlands. Spanish foot soldiers had already captured the king of France himself, at Pavia in 1525.

pages.x: In Germany the Protestant princes had joined in a league against the Catholic emperor. In April 1547 Charles and the Duke of Alba forded the Elbe at Mühlberg, routed the league's army and took its leader prisoner. Titian painted Charles riding to that battle in armour, alone, gaunt and calm, and set the pattern for royal portraits on horseback for centuries.

Worn out, Charles gave up his crowns in 1556. His brother Ferdinand, already ruler of Austria, became emperor, and his son Philip II took Spain, Italy, the Netherlands and the Americas. In 1580 Philip claimed Portugal and its empire too. One king now ruled from Mexico to Manila, and it was said that the sun never set on his lands.

Philip's heavy taxes and his burning of Protestants drove the Netherlands to revolt. In 1568 the Duke of Alba beheaded two great nobles, Egmont and Horn, in the main square of Brussels, and William of Orange led the rebels. Unpaid Spanish soldiers sacked Antwerp in 1576, and the northern provinces broke away to form the Dutch Republic.

On 7 October 1571 the fleet of the Holy League, mostly Spanish and Venetian, met the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras, off western Greece. Over 400 galleys fought it out in a few hours, one of the largest sea battles ever fought. The Christians won, led by Philip's young half-brother, Don John of Austria. Among the wounded was a Spanish soldier named Miguel de Cervantes.
Silver from the mines of Potosí and Mexico poured into Seville, and Philip spent it before it arrived, on armies in Italy and the Netherlands and fleets at sea, among them the Armada of 1588.
pages.fx: It was never enough. The crown went bankrupt in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596, unpaid soldiers mutinied, and the taxes fell hardest on Castile, which grew poorer as its king grew mightier.

pages.x: The war with the Dutch began again in 1621. In 1625 the Genoese general Ambrogio Spinola took the fortress of Breda after a siege of ten months, and ten years later Diego Velázquez painted him receiving its keys. Spinola lays a hand on the Dutch commander's shoulder instead of letting him kneel: Spanish pride, painted with a rare courtesy.

France joined the war against Spain in 1635, and in 1640 both Catalonia and Portugal rose against Madrid. In May 1643 a Spanish army invading France besieged the little fortress town of Rocroi. The French, led by the 21-year-old Duke of Enghien, broke the Spanish horsemen, and the veteran tercios stood their ground until most of them were killed or taken.

In 1659, on an island in a border river, Spain and France made the Peace of the Pyrenees. Philip IV gave up Roussillon and Artois, and his daughter married the young Louis XIV. Spain kept its empire for another 150 years, but the leadership of Europe had passed to France.
pts: Spain's kings ruled much of Europe and the Americas
The tercios were Europe's best soldiers for a century
In 1659 the lead in Europe passed to France
